## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

The code constructs authentication-related structures (authenticators, scheme.lower, hexdigest) and performs string manipulation (join, replace, split, startswith). The combination of credential-like variables (username, password) flowing into encoding/hashing operations with no documented legitimate purpose in a package named 'pygraphql32' is suspicious. The flow boundary is Vendor-Internal, and the sensitive API b64encode() is used on credential-adjacent data, which is consistent with credential obfuscation/exfiltration preparation.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B shows a top similarity of 1.00 to 'cheese-python3-api' (unclassified) and 'node-db-indicator' (supply_chain_downloader tag). However, 'requtils' carries specific tags: credential_stealer, data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer at 1.00 similarity. Per RULE 2, a specific non-generic attack tag at high similarity (≥0.85) is corroboration. The presence of credential_stealer and data_exfiltration tags on a 1.00-similarity match strongly corroborates the credential-handling anomaly found in Q1.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The specific anomaly is credential-like variables (username, password) being processed through base64 encoding and hashing operations with no documented legitimate purpose in the visible code, combined with a 1.00-similarity match to a confirmed credential_stealer/data_exfiltration package (requtils).

The matched package requtils is confirmed as credential_stealer, data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer.

policy_violations.violation_reason: Code uses base64 encoding on credential-adjacent data, consistent with obfuscation techniques flagged by this rule.

Base64 encoding of credential data is a form of obfuscation consistent with T1140.

mitre_mapping.relevance: Use of b64encode on credential-like strings indicates obfuscation of sensitive data.
Username and password variables are accessed and processed, suggesting credential harvesting.
Encoded credential data may be prepared for exfiltration, corroborated by similarity to data_exfiltration-tagged malware.

llm_evaluation.summary: The package pygraphql32 exhibits credential-handling behavior: username and password variables flow into base64 encoding and hashing operations with no documented legitimate purpose. Section B shows a 1.00 similarity to requtils, a confirmed credential_stealer and data_exfiltration package, providing specific-tag corroboration. The combination of unexplained credential processing and high-similarity match to confirmed credential-stealing malware leads to a MALICIOUS verdict with ATTEND confidence.

request-cache-py impersonates the legitimate requests-cache HTTP caching library. On `import request_cache_py`, the package's `__init__.py` starts a background thread that harvests installer-side secrets and POSTs them to a hardcoded attacker Telegram bot.

Observed behaviors:
- Reads private keys and credentials from `~/.ssh/` (`id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_dsa`), `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.dockercfg`, `~/.docker/config.json`, plus gcloud and vscode settings.
- Copies Chrome/Edge/Safari `Login Data`, `Cookies`, and `History` SQLite databases to `/tmp` and extracts saved logins, cookies, and browsing history (`SELECT origin_url, username_value FROM logins`; `SELECT host_key, name, value, path FROM cookies`).
- Iterates `os.environ` and exfiltrates any variable whose name contains `key`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `api`, or `auth`.
- Posts the collected data to `https://api.telegram.org/bot<redacted>/sendMessage` with a fixed `chat_id`. The bot token and chat id are base64-split across pieces and reassembled at runtime to evade scanners.
- Includes sandbox-evasion: `_should_skip()` aborts when `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `TRAVIS`, `JENKINS_HOME`, `CIRCLECI`, `/.dockerenv`, or hypervisor markers are present, restricting execution to real developer workstations. A `~/.cache/.pyrc` marker suppresses repeat sends within 24 hours.

The combination — name impersonation of a popular library, import-time credential harvest from classic developer secret paths, browser database theft, env scraping, base64-obfuscated C2, sandbox evasion — is a deliberate supply-chain credential stealer targeting human developers.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag

  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.

WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.

  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern

    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B

    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

setup.py registers install, develop, and egg_info command hooks that run a routine which XOR-0x5A-decodes a list of attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers hostnames (package-proxy.cf5oobworker.workers.dev and four sibling *.workers.dev hosts) and a URL path (/pkg/package), downloads opaque bytes over HTTPS, writes them to /var/tmp/.cache_<random>, chmods 0755, and spawns the binary detached via subprocess.Popen with start_new_session=True. If HTTPS fetch fails, it falls back to a DNS covert channel: raw DNS TXT queries against `*.lin.dl.wel1.ru` reassemble a base64 payload from serial subdomain lookups, which is then decoded and executed. The hook is wired into egg_info as well as install/develop, so the payload fires during `pip install` and even during metadata-only operations. The package itself has no real functionality — src/haproxy_config_client/__init__.py contains only a __version__ string — and its name plus 'Internal service utilities' summary and 'TBank Engineering' author label are consistent with a dependency-confusion vehicle targeting an internal ops utility.

## Source: kam193 (f70d07844bca4fadfcedb195f5768c8a95318af4d62a4bcec94556b99b72c4ad)

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.

WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.

  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B

    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag

The specific anomaly is: decoding and executing content whose purpose is never referenced elsewhere in the visible code, alongside environment variable access and file writes, which together form an unexplained install-time or import-time side effect chain.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B shows five matches at 0.97 similarity, all tagged 'data_exfiltration' with category 'network'. ## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot

Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

}

reasoning.code_intent: Section A shows a package that, during import, uses a hook mechanism (hook_data, hook(), req, PreparedRequest) to intercept or construct HTTP requests and then performs file operations (read, remove, append, extend, join) and string manipulation (decode, lower, startswith, keys, DEFAULT_PORTS.get). The data flows from string literals into attribute sinks and string sinks, indicating dynamic construction of paths or commands. The presence of PreparedRequest and hook() suggests request interception or modification, while the file operations (read, remove, append) indicate reading, deleting, and writing files. The combination of request hooking and file manipulation, especially with remove and append, is not explained by ordinary GraphQL library functionality. There is no visible documentation or legitimate reason for a GraphQL package to hook HTTP requests and manipulate files in this manner. The behavior is consistent with a backdoor or data exfiltration mechanism that intercepts requests, reads sensitive files, and exfiltrates or modifies data.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B shows a top similarity of 0.98 to 'timecurrently', which is tagged with backdoor, data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer, and supply_chain_downloader. Other matches include 'req7ests' (typosquatting), 'puregram' (data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer), and 'cncode'/'gui-build' (unclassified). The specific attack tags on multiple high-similarity matches corroborate the malicious intent found in Q1. The similarity is not merely generic shape overlap because the matched samples carry confirmed malicious classifications.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The specific anomaly is the combination of HTTP request hooking (PreparedRequest, hook()) and file operations (read, remove, append) that are not explained by the stated purpose of a GraphQL library. This behavior is consistent with data exfiltration and backdoor functionality.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in file operations, dynamic attribute access, and request handling patterns. The matched package is confirmed malicious with backdoor and data exfiltration tags.

policy_violations.violation_reason: The code uses dynamic attribute access and hook mechanisms to resolve and call functions at runtime, potentially to evade detection.
The hooking of HTTP requests and manipulation of file operations could be used to inject malicious code or data into processes.

mitre_mapping.relevance: The use of hook() and dynamic attribute access indicates obfuscation of API calls.
Request hooking and file manipulation may facilitate injection of malicious payloads.
The combination of request interception and file reading suggests potential data exfiltration.

llm_evaluation.summary: The package pygraphql32 exhibits malicious behavior by hooking HTTP requests and performing file operations (read, remove, append) that are not explained by its stated GraphQL functionality. The code dynamically constructs paths and commands, and the data flows indicate potential data exfiltration. Section B corroborates this with high similarity to known malware tagged as backdoor and data exfiltration. The verdict is MALICIOUS with high confidence, and the SSVC decision is ATTEND due to the specific anomaly and corroborating tags.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag

  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.

reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## Source: amazon-inspector (6f86ffde45262c5d45a24458a85116ab5ca80451ce3d3159f9d7cad6599ad145)
setup.py registers install, develop, and egg_info command hooks that run a routine which XOR-0x5A-decodes a list of attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers hostnames (package-proxy.cf5oobworker.workers.dev and four sibling *.workers.dev hosts) and a URL path (/pkg/package), downloads opaque bytes over HTTPS, writes them to /var/tmp/.cache_<random>, chmods 0755, and spawns the binary detached via subprocess.Popen with start_new_session=True. If HTTPS fetch fails, it falls back to a DNS covert channel: raw DNS TXT queries against `*.lin.dl.wel1.ru` reassemble a base64 payload from serial subdomain lookups, which is then decoded and executed. All C2 hostnames, the URL path, and dynamic-import module names ('base64', 'b64decode', 'b32encode') are XOR-obfuscated byte literals whose only purpose is to hide the destinations from review. The hook is wired into egg_info as well as install/develop, so the payload fires during `pip install` and even during metadata-only operations. The package itself has no real functionality — src/haproxy_config_client/__init__.py contains only a __version__ string — and its name plus 'Internal service utilities' summary and 'TBank Engineering' author label are consistent with a dependency-confusion vehicle targeting an internal ops utility.

## Source: kam193 (f70d07844bca4fadfcedb195f5768c8a95318af4d62a4bcec94556b99b72c4ad)
During installation the obfuscated code downloads a malicious executable from a remote location. This record returns a number, which is then used to iterate over domains in the form <0...n>.lin.dl.wel1[.]r and reconstruct the encoded executable from their TXT records. The executable is finally saved under a partially random name, executed, and removed after execution. ## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.
